title: How your mind tricks you
blurb: The shortcuts your brain takes, and the mistakes they cause.

cards.text: Your brain runs two kinds of thinking: one quick and automatic, one slow and effortful. Many mistakes happen when the quick one answers a question meant for the slow one.
Fast, automatic and always on. It reads a face, finishes “2 + 2 =” and swerves round a pothole before you’ve decided anything.
Slow and deliberate. It works out 17 × 24, fills in a form and checks an argument. Because it takes effort, it often lets System 1 lead.
A bat and a ball cost $1.10 in total. The bat costs $1 more than the ball. How much is the ball? Most people’s first answer is 10 cents.
The ideas come from psychologists Daniel Kahneman and Amos Tversky. Kahneman won the 2002 Nobel prize in economics and wrote Thinking, Fast and Slow (2011).

cards.q: So how much is the ball?
cards.explain: 5 cents. The bat is then $1.05, which is $1 more, and together they make $1.10.

points: System 2 is slow and takes effort
An answer that feels right can still be wrong

cards.text: The first number you see pulls your judgement towards it, even when it has nothing to do with the question. It’s called the anchoring effect.
In a 1974 study, Tversky and Kahneman spun a wheel rigged to land on 10 or 65, then asked what percentage of African countries were in the UN.
People who saw 10 gave a median guess of 25%. People who saw 65 guessed 45%. A random number had moved their answer.
Anchors show up in prices (“was £99, now £49”), salary talks and first offers in any negotiation. The first figure sets what feels reasonable.
Knowing about anchoring doesn’t make you immune: studies find experts are pulled by anchors too, and warnings only partly help.

cards.q: People who saw 65 on the wheel…
cards.explain: They guessed higher: a median of 45%, against 25% for people who saw 10.

points: The first number you see sticks
Anchors work even when they’re random
Decide your own number before you see theirs

cards.text: We look for, remember and favour information that fits what we already believe, and skim past what doesn’t.
In Peter Wason’s 1960 test, people had to find the rule behind 2, 4, 6. Most only tried numbers that fitted their guess, like 8, 10, 12.
The rule was simply numbers in ascending order. Few found it, because few tried a sequence that might prove them wrong.
We judge how likely something is by how easily examples come to mind. Vivid, recent or widely reported events feel more common than they are.
A useful habit: ask “what would show I’m wrong?” and go looking for exactly that.

cards.q: What was the hidden rule in Wason’s test?
cards.explain: Any ascending numbers. Testing 1, 2, 3 or 5, 20, 99 would have shown it.

points: We favour what we already believe
Look for the evidence that would prove you wrong

cards.text: Losing something hurts more than gaining the same thing feels good. Studies suggest losses weigh roughly twice as much as equal gains.
Kahneman and Tversky’s 1979 prospect theory describes how people actually choose under risk: from a reference point, with losses felt more than gains.
In a 1981 study, 72% chose a plan described as saving 200 of 600 people. Described as 400 of 600 dying, the same plan won 22%.
The same choice, worded as a gain or a loss, leads to different decisions. That’s the framing effect.
In the Second World War, statistician Abraham Wald saw that bullet holes on returning planes showed where a plane could be hit and survive. Armour was needed where they had none.

cards.q: Roughly how much stronger do losses feel than equal gains?
cards.explain: About twice as strong, in many studies.

points: Losses hurt more than gains please
How a choice is worded changes the answer
Think about what you can’t see, not just what you can
